title: Nobody knows it all
paras: Nobody knows it all. There's a quiet myth that the people who get on manage everything themselves, and it does real harm. In more than forty years I've never met a good planner who succeeded alone. The ones who lasted nearly always had a mentor to learn from, a network to lean on, and colleagues to turn to when a case had them stuck. It isn't a solitary craft — you're not meant to do it on your own, and those who seem to be are usually just hiding how much help they quietly get.

Planning is far too broad for anyone to master every corner. In a single week you might touch heritage, ecology, highways, enforcement, a neighbour dispute and a knotty point of policy — no one is expert in all of it. Even the most senior planner still picks up the phone on unfamiliar ground and wants a second opinion on a finely balanced call — not weakness, but why they're trusted. Needing advice isn't a phase you grow out of; the questions change, but the asking never stops. The worst mistakes I've seen came from planners who pressed on rather than admit they were unsure, when a five-minute conversation would have saved them.

The biggest influence on my early career wasn't a course — it was a senior planner who let me sit in on his difficult cases, talked me through how he reached a view, and never made me feel foolish for asking. The whole profession runs, quietly, on people taking that kind of time for one another.

title: What a mentor really is
paras: So what is a mentor, really? Just a more experienced planner who takes an interest in how you're getting on and shares what they've learned. Not a teacher, not a manager judging you — someone further down the road who'll talk things through honestly, tell you when you're on the right track and steer you when you're not, and let you learn from their mistakes rather than make all of your own. It can be formal, through a scheme, or entirely informal — a senior colleague whose door is always open.

And mentoring isn't only for trainees. The value of someone wiser to talk to doesn't run out when you pass your assessment; if anything the questions get harder as you go up — setting up on your own, taking on staff, weighing whether to fight an appeal. The best planners keep a mentor, or several, all their working lives, and become mentors themselves. There's little more satisfying in a long career than watching someone you helped become excellent in their own right.

title: The learning that is never in a textbook
paras: Then there's the learning that's never in a textbook. Policy and law you get from books and courses, but the craft — how to read a room at committee, break bad news to a client, sense when a scheme that ticks every box still isn't right — passes from person to person, mostly through ordinary conversation. That's where the real depth of the profession lives — you absorb it working alongside experienced people and talking through the cases without a tidy answer.

Talking a difficult case through is valuable quite apart from the advice. Explaining a knotty problem out loud, to someone who understands the work, often shows you the answer before they've said a word — and a good colleague asks the question you hadn't thought to ask yourself. Thinking aloud with people you trust is how you test a judgement before you commit and catch the flaw you were too close to see. The more freely a workplace allows those conversations, the better everyone becomes.

title: The people around you
paras: Now, the people around you. Beyond a mentor, every planner benefits from a wider circle — the professional network. In practice it's the handful of people, in other authorities and practices or met through professional life, you can ring with a question or turn to for a steer. When you hit something unfamiliar, the chances are someone in that circle has met it before, and a short conversation saves you hours.

Networks are worth tending — not for advancement, but because a profession is easier when you're part of it rather than facing it alone. The R-T-P-I and its branches exist partly for this, and the Young Planners networks do the same for those starting out. Going along, staying in touch, helping others when they come to you builds a web of support you'll be glad of on a difficult day. The planner with a good network is never really stuck; the one who's kept to themselves faces every problem cold.

title: Looking out for each other
paras: Which brings me to looking out for each other. Support runs in every direction, not just downwards. Experienced planners have a duty to bring on those behind them, generously and patiently. But senior people need support too, and often get less, because everyone assumes they're fine. The head of service carrying the department, the sole practitioner with no colleagues, the experienced planner having a hard year — they can be quietly struggling behind a competent front, and care aimed upwards matters more than we admit.

Part of it is noticing when a colleague doesn't seem themselves — gone quiet, staying late and looking worn, or lost their usual spark. When you notice, the kind thing is also the simple thing: a quiet, private word. You've seemed a bit weighed down lately; is everything all right? You're not there to diagnose or fix their life, only to let them know they've been seen, and to point them towards more formal help if they want it. Often, just being asked by someone who means it lets a person say they're finding things hard — usually the first step to things getting better.

title: Asking for help is professional
paras: Asking for help is professional — it's the one idea to pin above the desk. The instinct to hide difficulty, to pretend to a confidence you don't feel, to treat asking as an admission of inadequacy, is common in planning and entirely wrong. The professionals I most respect are the ones who say, without embarrassment, I'm not sure about this, let me check — or, this one's getting on top of me, can we talk it through? That's what competence sounds like. Worry instead about the one who never asks and never admits a doubt, because sooner or later they'll get something badly wrong rather than lose face.

And a team takes its cue from whether asking is safe. If the people at the top ask for help themselves, respond well when others do, and never punish uncertainty, then everyone below can too, and problems get raised while they're still small. Treat asking as failure and people hide their struggles until they become crises. Making it as normal to say I'm overloaded this week as to say I'm on top of things costs nothing but a change of attitude. The strongest teams aren't the ones where nobody needs help — they're the ones where asking for it is completely unremarkable.

title: A profession worth staying in
paras: All of this points to something bigger — a profession worth staying in. A supportive culture isn't built by grand initiatives; it's built by countless small acts — the experienced planner who makes time for a graduate, the colleague who talks a difficult case through, the manager who asks for help themselves and so makes it safe for the rest. Every planner adds to that culture, or detracts from it, by how they treat the people around them — and the kindness you show a newcomer today shapes the colleague they become in twenty years' time.

And it's worth remembering, in a demanding and sometimes bruising job, that planning is also genuinely rewarding, full of good people. You get to shape places, solve real problems, make a difference to how communities live — alongside colleagues who are overwhelmingly decent and generous when given half a chance. The planners who build long, happy careers are almost never the lone experts of the myth; they found good people to learn from, kept them around, and gave the same back. Look after the people around you, and let them look after you, and the work becomes something to enjoy for a lifetime. You are not alone in this — and you were never meant to be.

title: In short
paras: In short, then — the heart of it in one place.

First, no one masters all of planning; the most senior still ask and check, and the questions only get harder. Second, a mentor is an experienced planner who takes an interest — keep one, or several, all your career, not just as a trainee. Third, the best of the craft is never in a textbook; it passes person to person, so talk your cases through. Fourth, tend your network — a good one means you're never really stuck. Fifth, support runs upwards too: senior people, sole practitioners and heads of service struggle quietly behind a competent front while everyone assumes they're fine.

Sixth, notice, and have the quiet word — being asked is often enough to let someone say they're struggling. Seventh, asking for help is what competence sounds like; worry about the one who never asks. Eighth, teams take their cue from the top — when leaders ask for help themselves, problems surface while they're small. Ninth, use what the profession offers: the R-T-P-I, its branches and the Young Planners networks help you find people to learn from. Tenth, culture is built from small acts that decide, over a career, whether planning is a profession people stay in. And finally, you were never meant to do it alone — those with long, happy careers found good people to learn from, kept them around, and gave the same back.
